extracted.intended_audience: EPA regulators, administrative law judges, environmental lawyers, petitioners/commenters, and agency technical staff
extracted.subtask_short: petition for reconsideration of EPA rule
extracted.subtask_description: A legal and technical challenge to EPA’s Final Rule finding GHG regulation futile, focusing on the agency’s choice of baselines, modeling methods, comparative metrics (measurability, variability, 1% threshold), statistical treatments, and procedural defects (notice-and-comment and transparency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate baseline selection
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriate baseline for assessing the effects of EPA’s repeal of GHG rules is the complete absence of any GHG regulation (past, present, or future), not later standards the Agency is repealing (e.g., MY2026 standards) or approximations tied to prior regulatory choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is illogical to treat as a baseline the standards the Agency is simultaneously repealing; baselines must reflect the counterfactual that the rule itself eliminates. EPA’s use of a 50% reduction tied to the 2024 rules misattributes prior agency choices to inherent statutory limits. See discussion that a future Administrator might reasonably project greater reductions as technology advances (e.g., >99% reductions historically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate evaluation of specific prior rules with futility of all GHG regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The efficacy or reasonableness of the 2024 rules versus prior baselines may inform whether those rules were reasonable, but cannot be used to justify a blanket finding that any and all section 202(a) GHG emissions standards are futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA’s analysis must not generalize from an approximation tied to one regulatory choice to a categorical rule that all present and future GHG standards are futile and thus repeal all existing standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider potential for more protective future standards and technological progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory assessment must account for the possibility that future Administrators could set more protective standards as technology and costs evolve; current regulatory choices do not set inherent statutory limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should not treat reductions achievable by the 2024 rules as an upper bound; historical exercise of section 202(a) has produced increasingly protective standards and could achieve reductions greater than the 2024 rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and documentation of modeling inputs and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must fully document emissions inputs, scenario definitions, and the analyses performed (e.g., which emissions were modeled by year, how a '50% reduction' scenario was implemented) in the record (e.g., Temperature Memo, RIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record must allow reprodcution: it should show whether the Agency modeled a 50% reduction starting MY2027 each year or weighted reductions over time, and provide the actual emissions inputs. Absent such documentation, the methodology is arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of climate models (no ad hoc scaling of outputs)
rubrics_metrics.description: If using models like BRICK and FaIR, EPA must input the emissions scenario into those models rather than simply scaling modeled outputs from a different emissions scenario (e.g., multiplying outputs by 50%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA’s preamble admits pairing analytic tools not intended for a purpose; substituting sophisticated modeling tools with an exogenous back-of-the-napkin scaling to produce a desired result is arbitrary and cannot reasonably be claimed to represent impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use models within their intended scope and validate tool pairing
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cannot 'pair some analytic tools not intended for this purpose with other tools' and then assume the results translate with precision to health or welfare impacts; models must be used as intended and validated for the specific analytic purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where models are combined, the agency must explain and justify why the pairing is appropriate and how outputs map onto downstream impact metrics; unsupported pairings render illustrative results meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirement: notice-and-comment for new comparative metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of new metrics (e.g., 'range of measurability,' global temperature 'variability' from 2016-25, and a 1% de minimis threshold) in the Final Rule without prior notice and an opportunity for public comment is arbitrary and procedurally improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these metrics are critical to the futility finding, EPA must have included them in a rulemaking record subject to notice-and-comment. The record must also show how such metrics were derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and distinguish measurability, variability, and materiality
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must separately define 'variability' (physical fluctuations in the climate system), 'measurability' (epistemic/observational uncertainty in measuring climate variables), and 'materiality' (whether a change affects human health and welfare), and must not conflate them into a single 'margin of error.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variability is inherent to the climate system (ENSO, PDO, AMO, long-term trends). Measurability depends on observational coverage, inhomogeneities, instrumentation, and statistical infilling. Materiality concerns whether shifting the projected distribution by some amount produces meaningful welfare/health consequences (e.g., 1°C shift in the distribution). EPA's conflation of these concepts is conceptually wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparisons must address apples-to-apples (not compare impacts to unrelated measurement metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s practice of comparing projected regulatory impacts to measurement uncertainty or short-term variability can be an apples-to-oranges comparison unless the comparator metric is conceptually appropriate for assessing materiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an impact lies within measurement uncertainty, it can still be material if the policy shifts the whole distribution. EPA must explain why a given uncertainty/variability comparator implies futility for regulation, rather than assuming impacts below an arbitrary threshold are meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement uncertainty must be supported by cited sources
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must accurately report and properly cite the empirical estimates it relies on for measurement uncertainty (e.g., NOAA, NASA, dataset-specific uncertainty analyses); figures in the preamble must be traceable to materials in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners demonstrate EPA's cited NOAA sources do not contain the figures reported. If EPA relies on other sources, they must be in the record; otherwise the agency must reopen the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate temporal averaging for long-term policy impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: For long-lived regulatory policies with multi-decade impacts (e.g., fleet turnover >20 years), EPA should use multi-year averages (e.g., 5-year, 10-year, 30-year) when assessing measurability and variability rather than annual metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement uncertainty typically decreases with longer averaging windows (Berkeley Earth five-year and thirty-year uncertainties cited). EPA's choice of annual metrics may understate measurability for multi-decadal policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify timeframe selection and avoid cherry-picking
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must justify why a particular analysis window (e.g., 2016–2025) is appropriate; claiming futility based on a single arbitrarily chosen period is insufficient because results may be sensitive to the time window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because EPA asserts a facial futility of regulation, it must show the futility conclusion holds across a wide range of reasonable periods, not just a single period that happens to show high variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for trends when measuring variability (do not misuse standard deviation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When deriving a variability metric from temperature time series, EPA must account for the underlying increasing trend in temperatures; using a sample standard deviation on trending data misstates variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample SD treats observations as scatter around a stationary mean; for trending climate data this inflates variability. Better metrics account for trend (e.g., detrending, using longer averages, or other trend-aware variability measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the correct form of standard deviation given the data context
rubrics_metrics.description: If the analysis uses the full set of annual observations for a defined period (e.g., all years 2016-2025), EPA should use population standard deviation rather than sample standard deviation; if using a sample, the sample must be random and justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA’s use of sample SD when the entire set of years is known is statistically unsound; alternatively, if data are a sample of a broader period, EPA must justify sampling method and representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circular reasoning when using variability driven by emissions as a reason not to regulate emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cannot rely on elevated variability (in part caused by past emissions) as a rationale for declaring regulation futile, because the variability it cites may be a consequence of the emissions that regulation aims to reduce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a circular argument: the elevated variability during 2016-2025 is at least partly a result of high GHG concentrations; using that elevated variability to preclude regulation is logically inconsistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility requirement for modeled results
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must provide sufficient transparency and data so that petitioners and reviewers can reproduce the Agency’s modeled figures (temperature and sea level impacts) and verify calculations (e.g., Table values and percentages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners report inability to reproduce EPA’s exact values due to lack of transparency. The record must include model inputs, parameter choices, and provenance for model runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity and robustness analysis for key assumptions and parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Given how sensitive outcomes are to choice of datasets, statistical techniques, temporal windows, and assumptions, EPA must subject key methodological choices to sensitivity analysis and provide opportunity for comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners show that addressing flaws (trend accounting, averaging, SD choice) can reduce EPA’s variability metric dramatically (e.g., to 0.0193 °C). Agency must show results robust across reasonable alternative assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify and support any numeric de minimis threshold with precedent and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed 1% de minimis threshold should be justified and consistent with precedent; deriving such a bright-line without explanation is arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners argue the 1% threshold and EPA’s process for deriving it are arbitrary and inconsistent with precedent; agency must show legal and technical support for adopting this threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate comparators for sea level rise measurability
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing projected sea level rise impacts to measurability, EPA must identify and justify the measurement uncertainty values (e.g., NASA reports ~4 mm/yr or 0.4 cm) and explain the basis for any larger values it claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners note EPA implies measurability exceeds 1.4 cm but cites no methodology; comparing 1.4 cm to NASA’s ~0.4 cm shows EPA’s projected impacts exceed measurement uncertainty when properly computed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish measurement uncertainty from policy materiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurability (uncertainty around estimates) is not equivalent to materiality (whether a reduction affects health/welfare); an impact smaller than observational uncertainty can still be material if it shifts projected outcomes in ways that affect risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a 1-degree reduction shifts the entire 60±2° projection band to 59±2°, which is materially different; EPA’s conflation of these concepts is conceptually wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on undocumented or post-hoc sources to justify record gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: If EPA intends to rely on additional sources (e.g., later studies reporting higher measurement uncertainty) those sources must be in the administrative record and subject to notice-and-comment; post-hoc citations cannot cure a defective record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners state that any such sources not in the final rule cannot cure procedural error and that agency must convene reconsideration if it intends to rely on them.
